title: "Main"
format: html

Communication is a tango; it takes two partners, requires continuous effort, and when one fails, the other may work harder to keep the dance alive. When communication fails, partners may not only repeat themselves, but also speak louder or gesture more extensively -- in other words, they might increase their communicative effort to become understood. Although communicative effort is so central to everyday multimodal communication, its physical dimension is largely unexplored. The current pre-registered study investigates whether communicative behavior that people engage in to (re)gain understanding is associated with an increase in physical effort. 

Across locomotion, arm-reaching, and decision-making, actions emerge from the continuous negotiation of metabolic, computational, cognitive, and biomechanical constraints [@BernsteinCoordinationRegulation1967; @kelsoDynamicPatternsSelforganization1995; @tverskyJudgmentUncertaintyHeuristics1974; @ferrer-i-canchoCompressionUniversalPrinciple2013; @rosenOptimalityPrinciplesBiology1967; @mcallisterBehaviouralEnergeticsHuman2025; @koolDecisionMakingAvoidance2010]. This is similarly true for  language: the way that people speak and structure their utterances reflects effort, particularly the optimization toward low-cost solutions [@gibsonHowEfficiencyShapes2019; @levshinaCommunicativeEfficiencyLanguage2022; @levshinaEfficiencyHumanLanguages2021; @zipfHumanBehaviorPrinciple1949]. 

In linguistics, effort has been operationalized primarily in terms of message length and information structure. Short, frequent forms require less articulation and place fewer demands on processing [@zipfHumanBehaviorPrinciple1949], and this principle has been shown to shape lexical frequency, word order, syntactic structure, sound duration, and articulatory detail across languages [@aylettSmoothSignalRedundancy2004; @bellPredictabilityEffectsDurations2009; @futrellLargescaleEvidenceDependency2015; @haspelmathExplainingGrammaticalCoding2021]. In speech sciences, physical effort has been used to explain why vocal targets are regularly not fully realized, resulting in phonetic reductions [@kirchnerEffortBasedApproach2001; @lindblomExplainingPhoneticVariation1990]. What these traditions have in common is that they have focused almost exclusively on the structure and production of spoken language, with a few exceptions extending these accounts to sign [@napoliLinguisticEffectsArticulatory2014; @slonimskaSimultaneityEmergentProperty2022]. 

Yet, language is fundamentally multimodal, distributed across, e.g., hand gestures, eye gaze, facial expressions, head nods, postural sway [@emmendorferFacialSignalsShape2025; @notaFacialSignalsSocial2021; @shockleyMutualInterpersonalPostural2003; @terbekkeGesturesSpeedResponses2024], and each of these bodily signals emerges from movement shaped by the constraints of human physiology 
[@kadavaCommunicatingHeadToeaccepted]. Speech is shaped by breathing [@fuchsRespiratoryFoundationsSpoken2021] and the biomechanics of the tongue and mandible [@macneilageOriginInternalStructure2000]; head and arm gestures involve substantial mass that interacts with body systems crucial for vocalization, such as the larynx [@cwiekScopeLimitsIconicaccepted] and the lungs [@pouwEnergyFlowsGesturespeech2020]; and the forces these movements generate are integral to their communicative function [@krebsSignLanguageEncodes2025]. Finally, posture provides the stable foundation on which all these bodily signals depend [@massionMovementPostureEquilibrium1992]. Movement is therefore a primary component of communication, and like all movement, it carries a physical cost. 

What distinguishes communicative movement from other types of movement (e.g., reaching) is that it is a signal produced for someone. Lindblom’s [@lindblomExplainingPhoneticVariation1990] H\&H Theory captured this as a trade-off between biological (optimizing) processes and environmental constraints, positioning behavior on a continuum between hypo- and hyper-articulation. Here, we extend this framework to the whole communicating body: the same trade-off applies not only to the vocal tract but to gesture, posture, and the biomechanical signals that together constitute multimodal communication. Hyper-articulation in this sense has been reported across communicative contexts such as infant-directed speech and gesture [@biersackFinetuningSpeechRegisters2005; @songEffectsAcousticProperties2010; @rohlfingWhichMotioneseParameters2022; @brandInfantsPreferMotionese2008]; pantomime [@zywiczynskiPraxisDemonstrationPantomime2023]; speech addressed to non-native or hearing-impaired interlocutors [@knollCanYouHear2015; @smithPROSODICACCOMMODATIONFRENCH2007; @beecheyHearingImpairmentIncreases2020]; and communication in background noise [@garnierSpeakingNoiseHow2014; @dohenCoProductionSpeechPointing2017; @trujilloSpeakersExhibitMultimodal2021].

A particularly revealing window into how this trade-off is realized in social interaction comes from repair, i.e., the moments when understanding breaks down and must be restored [@schegloffPreferenceSelfcorrectionOrganization1977; @dingemanseUniversalPrinciplesRepair16.9.2015]. Unlike noise or perceptual impairment, repair imposes an epistemic constraint: the signal was received, but its meaning is not shared. Speakers add more detail to their gestures when they recognize a lack of shared understanding [@hilliardBridgingGapsCommon2016], produce more submovements, and use more orthographic characters when attempting to regain it [@rasenbergMultimodalNatureCommunicative2022]. Addressee’s feedback can also cause gestures to increase in rate [@hoetjesWhatHappensGesture2015] and become more precisely articulated than their previous occurrence [@hollerExperimentalInvestigationHow2011, see @hollerChapter10Multimodal2017 for a review]. The opposite applies when common ground is established: gestures become shorter [@hollerGivennewEffectsDuration2022], smaller in amplitude and less precise [@gerwingLinguisticInfluencesGestures2004], or less frequent [@hollerEffectCommonGround2007; @parrillHandsArePart2010]. However, this body of work has typically framed these adaptations in terms of clarity, informativity, or perceptual robustness rather than physical effort itself, and has relied on qualitative observation or surface kinematic and acoustic proxies rather than direct biomechanical measurement. The physical costs of communicative whole-body movement in repair, and how that cost is distributed across voice, limbs, and posture as a coordinated whole, therefore, remains underexplored.

In the current study, we test whether the modulations that people make in their communicative behavior to regain understanding are associated with an increase in physical effort. We define physical effort as an energetic cost of an action [@halperinIntegratedPerspectiveEffort2024] associated with the enhancement of (a feature of) an articulator [@lindblomExplainingPhoneticVariation1990], and treat increased effortfulness as a shift from a low-cost baseline toward hyper-articulation. To measure physical effort directly rather than approximate it through surface behavior, we combine the acoustic amplitude envelope, which reflects subglottal pressure and respiratory engagement [@zhangCauseeffectRelationshipVocal2016; @fuchsRespiratoryFoundationsSpoken2021; @pouw_etal23], with two biomechanical indices drawn from movement science: net joint torque change for upper-limb movement [@unoFormationControlOptimal1989] and change in center of pressure (COPc) for postural adjustments [@winterHumanBalancePosture1995]. Both have been linked to energetic expenditure [@mohammadzadehgonabadiGroundReactionForces2024] and, unlike kinematic proxies, account for the masses being moved and the dynamic demands of maintaining balance. We further distinguish *instantaneous* effort, the peak exertion at local moments, from *cumulative* effort, the total physical cost accumulated over a performance. 

We test two pre-registered hypotheses. In our referential task design, each failed guess triggers an obligatory correction attempt, posing an output-oriented constraint that calls for hyper-articulated behavior [@lindblomExplainingPhoneticVariation1990]. We predict that *correction recruits more physical effort than baseline performance* (H1). Because interlocutors are known to exploit shared knowledge to calibrate their multimodal behavior [@gerwingLinguisticInfluencesGestures2004; @hilliardBridgingGapsCommon2016; @hollerExperimentalInvestigationHow2011; @levshinaCommunicativeEfficiencyLanguage2022], we further predict that *a higher degree of misunderstanding recruits more physical effort from the performer* (H2). Because communicative modality determines which articulators are available for elaboration, we additionally examine how effort levels and communicative outcomes differ across unimodal and multimodal conditions – asking whether having access to both gesture and voice saves effort, improves success, or both. In an exploratory analysis that was not pre-registered, we further ask whether the effort invested in repair translates into better communicative outcomes, a question that, to our knowledge, has not been systematically examined. Across the three modalities, we find that in communicative repair, performers recruit sustained but not greater peak effort, a pattern that reflects elaboration of the message rather than amplification of its parts. This distinction reframes effortful repair as the production of *more* communicative material rather than the same material delivered more intensely, with implications for how the body coordinates to sustain mutual understanding.
